Melchizedek
mel-KIZ-ih-dek
proper noun
Hebrew Malkī-Tsedek, “king of righteousness,” from melek (king) + tsedek (righteousness). King of Salem and priest of the Most High God who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings (Gen 14:18-20); typological figure of Christ’s priestly office in Psalm 110 and developed at length in Hebrews 5-7.

See also: Melchizedek

📖 Biblical Definition

Melchizedek is one of the most theologically substantive minor figures in the entire Bible—a king-priest of Salem who appears suddenly in Genesis 14:18-20 to meet Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, blesses Abraham, receives from Abraham a tenth of all the spoil, and then disappears from the OT narrative without genealogy, birth-or-death notice, or subsequent appearance. The narrative is brief but theologically dense. Genesis 14:18-20: and Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God. And he blessed him, and said, Blessed be Abram of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth: And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand. And he gave him tithes of all. Psalm 110:4 takes up the Melchizedek figure and develops it Messianically: the LORD hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. The verse is one of the great Messianic prophecies, identifying the coming Messiah as a priest of a different order than the Aaronic priesthood. Hebrews 5-7 develops the doctrine at greatest length, with Hebrews 7 as the structural climax. Several features emerge. First, the king-priest combination. Melchizedek is both king (of Salem) and priest (of the Most High God); the two offices, separated under the Mosaic economy (the priests from Aaron’s line, the kings from David’s line), are united in Melchizedek as a typological prefiguring of the Messiah-King-Priest. Second, the order distinct from Aaron. Hebrews 7 argues at length that the Melchizedekian priesthood is of a different (and superior) order than the Aaronic. Melchizedek met Abraham before the Levitical priesthood existed; Abraham (and through him Levi) paid tithes to Melchizedek, indicating Melchizedek’s superiority; the Aaronic priesthood is therefore inferior to the Melchizedekian order. Third, the without-genealogy detail. Hebrews 7:3: without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life; but made like unto the Son of God; abideth a priest continually. The point is not that Melchizedek was literally without parents or birth (that would make him a divine figure not a historical person), but that the narrative omits these details deliberately, making him a typological figure resembling the eternal Son of God. Fourth, the bread-and-wine. Melchizedek’s bringing forth of bread and wine to meet Abraham has been read across church history as a typological anticipation of Christ’s institution of the Lord’s Supper with bread and wine. Fifth, the supreme NT fulfillment. Christ Himself is the eternal King-Priest after the order of Melchizedek, fulfilling Psalm 110:4. His priesthood is superior to the Aaronic; His office combines king-and-priest in one Person; He has no genealogy that establishes His priestly right (His priesthood is by divine appointment, not by Aaronic lineage); He abides a priest continually in the eternal heavens. The Melchizedek-doctrine is therefore one of the most extended typological developments in Scripture, occupying three full chapters of Hebrews to set forth Christ’s priesthood in its eternal, king-priest, Melchizedekian character.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 describes MELCHIZEDEK as a king of Salem and priest of the most high God (Gen 14:18); in scripture, a typological figure of Christ’s eternal king-priest office, developed at length in Psalm 110:4 and Hebrews 5-7 as the basis for Christ’s superior priesthood distinct from and surpassing the Aaronic order.

MELCHIZEDEK — A king of Salem and priest of the most high God who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings (Gen 14:18-20); typological figure of Christ’s eternal king-priest office (Ps 110:4; Heb 5-7).

PRIESTHOOD, n. — The office or character of a priest; in scripture, the Aaronic priesthood (established with Aaron and his sons), and the higher Melchizedekian priesthood fulfilled in Christ.

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 14:18-20 — "And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God. And he blessed him, and said, Blessed be Abram of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth: And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand. And he gave him tithes of all."

Psalm 110:4 — "The LORD hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek."

Hebrews 7:1-3 — "For this Melchisedec, king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, and blessed him; To whom also Abraham gave a tenth part of all; first being by interpretation King of righteousness, and after that also King of Salem, which is, King of peace; Without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life; but made like unto the Son of God; abideth a priest continually."

Hebrews 7:24-25 — "But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood. Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Melchizedek-doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the over-extension that has identified Melchizedek as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ Himself (against Hebrews 7:3’s language of made like unto the Son of God, distinguishing the type from the antitype)—and on the other by the general loss of attention to Hebrews 5-7’s extended development of the doctrine in much contemporary preaching, which leaves the priesthood-of-Christ taught only in its general outlines without the Melchizedekian substance.

expand to see more

The over-extension that identifies Melchizedek as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ Himself has appeared in various church-historical contexts (and is taught by some today). The reasoning typically goes: Hebrews 7:3 describes Melchizedek as without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life—these features fit only the divine Christ; therefore Melchizedek must be a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ in Genesis 14. The reading misses Hebrews 7:3’s actual language: Melchizedek is made like unto the Son of God—not the Son Himself, but resembling Him in the features the OT narrative deliberately includes (no genealogy, no beginning, no end mentioned). The point is typological resemblance, not identity. The orthodox tradition has consistently distinguished the type (Melchizedek, a historical king-priest of Salem) from the antitype (Christ, the eternal King-Priest after Melchizedek’s order). To identify them is to lose the typological structure Hebrews 7 carefully establishes; to distinguish them is to preserve both the substantive resemblance and the proper Christ-type distinction.

The opposite corruption is the general loss of attention to Hebrews 5-7’s extended development of the Melchizedek-doctrine in much contemporary preaching. The doctrine of Christ’s priesthood is taught (often briefly) in its general outlines—He is our great High Priest, He intercedes for us, He has offered Himself as the sacrifice—without the Melchizedekian substance that distinguishes Christ’s priesthood from the Aaronic and grounds it in the eternal king-priest figure of Genesis 14 and Psalm 110:4. The recovery is the recovery of careful Hebrews 5-7 preaching, which develops the Melchizedek-doctrine as the structural foundation for several substantive Christological claims: Christ’s priesthood is eternal (not generational like Aaron’s); His office combines king-and-priest (united in Him as in Melchizedek); His priesthood is superior to the Aaronic (as the writer argues at length from the Abraham-Melchizedek-Levi-tithes argument); He saves to the uttermost because He ever lives to make intercession. The Melchizedek-doctrine is therefore not antiquarian curiosity but the structural foundation for the doctrine of Christ’s unique and superior priesthood, on which much of Christian assurance depends.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Malkī-Tsedek (king of righteousness), king of Salem and priest of the Most High God (Gen 14:18-20); typological figure of Christ’s eternal king-priest office developed in Psalm 110:4 and Hebrews 5-7; Christ is the eternal Priest after the order of Melchizedek, whose priesthood is eternal, king-priest-unified, superior to Aaron, and the foundation of His saving to the uttermost through perpetual intercession.

Hebrew Malkī-Tsedek (H4442) — Melchizedek (literally king of righteousness; 2 OT uses: Gen 14:18; Ps 110:4).

Greek Melchisedek (G3198) — Melchizedek (8 NT uses, all in Hebrews 5-7).

Hebrew Shālēm (H8004) — Salem (Gen 14:18; Ps 76:2; identified with Jerusalem).

Greek archiereus (G749) — high priest (Christ as the Great High Priest after the order of Melchizedek).
